desc:
The subtree sum of a node is the sum of the values of the node and all of its descendants. Every node of the tree has one subtree sum, and different nodes may share the same one.

Return every subtree sum that occurs the largest number of times among all nodes. If several sums tie for the highest frequency, return all of them. The returned array must be sorted in ascending order.

How trees are given. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order (top to bottom, left to right). The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn; a missing child is written as -1 (real node values are never negative). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped.

For example, [1,2,3,-1,4] is the tree whose root 1 has children 2 and 3; node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child; node 3 is a leaf.

Example 1

tree = [5,2,3]
Output: [2,3,10]
The subtree sums are 2, 3 and 10, each occurring once.

Example 2

tree = [2,1,1]
Output: [1]
The sums are 1, 1 and 4; the sum 1 occurs twice.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly
Return the sums in ascending order
hints: First work out how to get the subtree sum of every node in one pass instead of re-summing each subtree separately.
The sum of a subtree is the node's value plus the sums of its two child subtrees, so a bottom-up sweep produces every subtree sum exactly once.
Count how often each sum appears in a hash map while sweeping, then take the maximum count and collect all sums that reach it. Sort them before returning.
editorial: Compute S(u) = val[u] + S(left) + S(right) for all nodes in one backwards sweep over the level-order array (children have larger indices than parents). Each computed value is added to a frequency counter.

After the sweep, find the highest frequency and return all sums with that frequency in ascending order. Time is O(n + d log d), where d is the number of distinct sums, and memory is O(n). Because values are non-negative, several nodes can share a sum (for example a node with a single child of value 0 and its child), which is why ties and the sorted output matter.
